blocks.text: An expedition climber has spent two days above 6000 m eating almost nothing. His glycogen stores are long gone, yet he keeps moving, and by the second day his breath carries a faint smell of acetone. His muscles are burning fat, and his liver is converting some of it into water-soluble fuels for his brain. Fat is the body's largest energy reserve, and the pathways that break it down and build it up are controlled so that they never run at the same time.

blocks.markdown: Fatty acids are stored as triacylglycerol in adipose tissue. During fasting, hormone-sensitive lipase releases free fatty acids, which travel in blood bound to albumin and are taken up by tissues such as muscle, heart and liver. Fatty acid **oxidation** extracts energy by repeatedly removing two-carbon units as acetyl-CoA; fatty acid **synthesis** builds long chains from acetyl-CoA when energy is in surplus. The two pathways are separated by location and regulated reciprocally.

blocks.title: Beta-oxidation
blocks.text: Beta-oxidation is the mitochondrial pathway that shortens a fatty acyl-CoA by two carbons per cycle, releasing acetyl-CoA, FADH2 and NADH. It is called beta-oxidation because the oxidation occurs at the beta-carbon (carbon 3) of the fatty acid.

blocks.markdown: **Step 1: activation and the carnitine shuttle.** In the cytosol (outer mitochondrial membrane) a fatty acid is activated to its CoA ester by **acyl-CoA synthetase**, using ATP (ATP becomes AMP + PPi, equal to the cost of 2 ATP). Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so its acyl group is carried across by **carnitine**: **carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I)** on the outer membrane transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine; a translocase carries acyl-carnitine into the matrix in exchange for free carnitine; **CPT-II** on the inner membrane transfers the acyl group back to CoA. CPT-I is the **rate-limiting, regulated step** and is inhibited by **malonyl-CoA**, the first committed intermediate of fatty acid synthesis.

**Step 2: the four reactions of beta-oxidation.** Each cycle in the matrix has four steps: (1) **acyl-CoA dehydrogenase** forms a trans double bond and produces **FADH2**; (2) **enoyl-CoA hydratase** adds water; (3) **3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase** oxidises the hydroxyl group and produces **NADH**; (4) **thiolase** cleaves off **acetyl-CoA**, leaving an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter that re-enters the cycle. For a saturated fatty acid with n carbons, there are (n/2 - 1) cycles and n/2 acetyl-CoA molecules.

blocks.caption: Beta-oxidation of palmitate (16 carbons): 7 cycles, 8 acetyl-CoA.

blocks.title: Net ATP from complete oxidation of palmitate
blocks.prompt: Using 10 ATP per acetyl-CoA (through the citric acid cycle and respiratory chain), 1.5 ATP per FADH2, 2.5 ATP per NADH, and 2 ATP-equivalents for activation, calculate the net ATP from complete oxidation of palmitic acid (16 carbons).

steps.text: Number of cycles = 16/2 - 1 = 7. Products: 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH2 and 7 NADH.
ATP from acetyl-CoA: 8 x 10 = 80. From FADH2: 7 x 1.5 = 10.5. From NADH: 7 x 2.5 = 17.5.
Sum and subtract the activation cost.

blocks.answer: Net yield is about 106 ATP per palmitate (older textbooks give 129 using higher per-coenzyme values).

blocks.markdown:
**Fatty acid synthesis** occurs in the **cytosol** (mainly liver, adipose tissue and lactating mammary gland) and uses acetyl-CoA that has left the mitochondrion as **citrate**; cytosolic ATP-citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA. The committed, rate-limiting step is **acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)**, a biotin-requiring enzyme that converts acetyl-CoA to **malonyl-CoA** using ATP and CO2. **Fatty acid synthase** then adds two-carbon units from malonyl-CoA, one at a time, to a growing chain, using **NADPH** as the reductant, until palmitate (16 carbons) is made: one acetyl-CoA primer and 7 malonyl-CoA give palmitate. NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway and from malic enzyme.

**Regulation.** ACC is **activated by insulin** (dephosphorylation) and by **citrate** (a sign of energy surplus), and **inhibited by glucagon and adrenaline** (via phosphorylation, including by AMP-activated protein kinase) and by long-chain acyl-CoA (palmitoyl-CoA). When ACC is active, malonyl-CoA also blocks CPT-I, so newly made fat is not immediately burned: the two pathways cannot run simultaneously.

rows: Mitochondrial matrix (and peroxisomes for very long chains)
Acyl carrier protein domain of fatty acid synthase
Produces FADH2 and NADH (NAD+ and FAD used)
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (activated by insulin and citrate)
blocks.caption: Fatty acid oxidation and synthesis contrasted.

blocks.markdown: **Ketone bodies in prolonged fasting.** When fasting lowers insulin and raises glucagon, adipose lipolysis rises and the liver oxidises large amounts of fatty acid. Oxaloacetate is drawn into gluconeogenesis, so acetyl-CoA exceeds the capacity of the citric acid cycle. Two acetyl-CoA condense (thiolase) to **acetoacetyl-CoA**; mitochondrial **HMG-CoA synthase** (the rate-limiting step) adds a third acetyl-CoA to make HMG-CoA; **HMG-CoA lyase** releases **acetoacetate**. Acetoacetate is reduced to **beta-hydroxybutyrate** (NADH-dependent) or spontaneously loses CO2 to **acetone**. Ketone bodies are released into blood and oxidised by muscle, heart and, after several days of starvation, the brain, which cannot use fatty acids. Tissues convert acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA using **succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase)**; the **liver lacks this enzyme**, so it makes ketone bodies but cannot use them.

blocks.title: Tracing carbon from fat to ketone bodies
blocks.prompt: A 12-carbon saturated fatty acid (laurate) is oxidised in the liver of a fasting patient. How many acetyl-CoA are formed, and how many acetoacetate molecules could be produced if all the acetyl-CoA were used for ketogenesis?

steps.text: Laurate has 12 carbons, so it yields 12/2 = 6 acetyl-CoA after (12/2 - 1) = 5 cycles.

Making one acetoacetate needs three acetyl-CoA (two condense to acetoacetyl-CoA, one more is added to form HMG-CoA, and one acetyl-CoA is released again by HMG-CoA lyase, so the net cost is two acetyl-CoA).
The net stoichiometry is therefore 2 acetyl-CoA per acetoacetate: 6 / 2 = 3 acetoacetate.

blocks.answer: 6 acetyl-CoA, giving at most 3 acetoacetate molecules.

items: Activation by acyl-CoA synthetase in the cytosol; carnitine (CPT-I, translocase, CPT-II) carries long-chain acyl groups into mitochondria.
Beta-oxidation cycle: dehydrogenation (FADH2), hydration, dehydrogenation (NADH), thiolytic cleavage (acetyl-CoA).
Synthesis is cytosolic, uses NADPH and malonyl-CoA; acetyl-CoA carboxylase is its regulated step.
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, separating the two pathways.
Liver makes ketone bodies; it cannot use them because it lacks thiophorase.

blocks.title: Why the brain needs ketone bodies
blocks.text: Fatty acids are bound to albumin and do not enter the brain in useful amounts, so during prolonged fasting the brain relies on glucose and, increasingly, on ketone bodies made by the liver, which reduces the amount of glucose (and therefore muscle protein) that has to be mobilised.

points: Beta-oxidation in mitochondria shortens acyl-CoA by two carbons per cycle, releasing acetyl-CoA, FADH2 and NADH; carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups across the inner membrane, with CPT-I as the regulated step.
Fatty acid synthesis is cytosolic, uses malonyl-CoA and NADPH, and is controlled by acetyl-CoA carboxylase (insulin and citrate activate it).
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I so synthesis and oxidation do not run together.
In prolonged fasting the liver converts surplus acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, which peripheral tissues and the brain use.

questions.stem: What is the role of carnitine in fatty acid oxidation?

options.text: It carries long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane
It activates fatty acids to acyl-CoA in the cytosol
It acts as the electron acceptor in the first step of beta-oxidation
It carries acetyl-CoA out of the mitochondrion as citrate

questions.correctOptionText: It carries long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane

distractorRationale.a: Correct: carnitine accepts the acyl group from CoA via CPT-I and returns it to CoA via CPT-II inside the matrix.
distractorRationale.b: Activation is carried out by acyl-CoA synthetase using ATP.
distractorRationale.c: FAD is the electron acceptor of acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
distractorRationale.d: Citrate, not carnitine, carries acetyl units out for fatty acid synthesis.

questions.explanation: Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Carnitine accepts the acyl group (CPT-I), a translocase carries acyl-carnitine across, and CPT-II returns the acyl group to CoA in the matrix.

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, hepatic fatty acid oxidation falls even though fatty acids are available. Which mechanism is mainly responsible?

options.text: Malonyl-CoA, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, inhibits CPT-I
Insulin inhibits thiolase directly
NADPH inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Glucagon inhibits acyl-CoA synthetase

questions.correctOptionText: Malonyl-CoA, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, inhibits CPT-I

distractorRationale.a: Correct: in the fed state insulin activates ACC, malonyl-CoA accumulates and blocks entry of fatty acids into mitochondria.
distractorRationale.b: Insulin does not directly inhibit thiolase.
distractorRationale.c: NADPH is used in synthesis and does not inhibit acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
distractorRationale.d: Glucagon is a signal for fasting and promotes oxidation.

questions.explanation: Insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, so malonyl-CoA rises. Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, preventing acyl groups from entering mitochondria, so newly synthesised fat is not burned straight away.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts fatty acid synthesis with beta-oxidation?

options.text: Synthesis is cytosolic and uses NADPH, whereas oxidation is mitochondrial and produces FADH2 and NADH
Synthesis is mitochondrial and uses NADH, whereas oxidation is cytosolic and uses NADPH
Both pathways occur in the cytosol and use the same enzymes in reverse
Synthesis removes acetyl-CoA from the chain and oxidation adds malonyl-CoA

questions.correctOptionText: Synthesis is cytosolic and uses NADPH, whereas oxidation is mitochondrial and produces FADH2 and NADH

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the pathways differ in location, carriers and redox coenzymes.
distractorRationale.b: This reverses the locations and coenzymes.
distractorRationale.c: The pathways use different enzymes, in different compartments.
distractorRationale.d: This reverses the roles: oxidation removes acetyl-CoA, synthesis adds malonyl-CoA units.

questions.explanation: Fatty acid synthesis is a cytosolic pathway using malonyl-CoA, fatty acid synthase and NADPH. Oxidation occurs in mitochondria and generates FADH2, NADH and acetyl-CoA. Separate compartments allow independent regulation.

questions.stem: Which hormonal state most strongly favours hepatic ketone body synthesis?

options.text: Low insulin and high glucagon, as in prolonged fasting
High insulin and low glucagon, as after a meal
High insulin and high glucagon together
Low insulin and low glucagon

questions.correctOptionText: Low insulin and high glucagon, as in prolonged fasting

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lipolysis rises, malonyl-CoA falls, CPT-I is active and oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis.
distractorRationale.b: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, favouring synthesis and blocking oxidation.
distractorRationale.d: Without glucagon the liver does not shift to gluconeogenesis and fat oxidation.

questions.explanation: Low insulin and high glucagon release fatty acids from adipose tissue, lower malonyl-CoA so that CPT-I is active, and promote gluconeogenesis, which uses oxaloacetate. The liver then has more acetyl-CoA than the cycle can handle and converts it to ketone bodies.

questions.stem: The liver produces large amounts of acetoacetate during fasting but cannot oxidise it for its own energy. Which enzyme deficiency in the liver explains this?

options.text: Liver lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase)
Liver lacks HMG-CoA synthase
Liver lacks acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Liver lacks HMG-CoA lyase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: without it acetoacetate cannot be converted back to acetoacetyl-CoA, so it is exported.
distractorRationale.b: HMG-CoA synthase is the enzyme the liver uses to make ketone bodies.
distractorRationale.c: The liver oxidises fatty acids by beta-oxidation using acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
distractorRationale.d: HMG-CoA lyase releases acetoacetate in the liver, so it is present.

questions.explanation: Peripheral tissues activate acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA using thiophorase, with succinyl-CoA as CoA donor. The liver lacks this enzyme, so it can make but not use ketone bodies, and exports them to other tissues.

questions.stem: Fatty acid synthesis needs acetyl-CoA in the cytosol, but acetyl-CoA is made inside mitochondria and cannot cross the inner membrane directly. How does it reach the cytosol?

options.text: As citrate, which is cleaved in the cytosol by ATP-citrate lyase
As acyl-carnitine, carried by CPT-I
As acetoacetate, converted back by thiophorase in the cytosol
As malonyl-CoA, formed inside the mitochondrion

questions.correctOptionText: As citrate, which is cleaved in the cytosol by ATP-citrate lyase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: citrate is exported and ATP-citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA in the cytosol.
distractorRationale.b: Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups into mitochondria for oxidation, not acetyl units out.
distractorRationale.c: Acetoacetate is a ketone body made for export from the liver; it is not the route for synthesis.
distractorRationale.d: Malonyl-CoA is made in the cytosol by acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

questions.explanation: In the fed state mitochondrial citrate accumulates and is exported to the cytosol, where ATP-citrate lyase releases acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. The acetyl-CoA is then carboxylated to malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which citrate also activates.

questions.stem: True or false: acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which makes malonyl-CoA, is activated by insulin and by citrate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase by promoting its dephosphorylation, and citrate, a signal of abundant acetyl-CoA and energy, activates it allosterically. Glucagon and palmitoyl-CoA inhibit it.

questions.stem: Stearic acid (18 carbons, saturated) is completely oxidised by a muscle cell. Using 10 ATP per acetyl-CoA, 1.5 ATP per FADH2, 2.5 ATP per NADH and a 2 ATP-equivalent cost of activation, calculate the net ATP yield per molecule.
questions.explanation: An 18-carbon chain undergoes 18/2 - 1 = 8 cycles and gives 9 acetyl-CoA, 8 FADH2 and 8 NADH. ATP: 9 x 10 = 90, 8 x 1.5 = 12 and 8 x 2.5 = 20, a total of 122. Subtracting 2 for activation gives 120 ATP.

questions.stem: Outline the oxidation of a saturated long-chain fatty acid, from entry into the cell to the release of acetyl-CoA, explaining the role of carnitine and naming the four reactions of each cycle.
markingGuide: Activation to acyl-CoA by acyl-CoA synthetase in the cytosol, using ATP
Carnitine shuttle: CPT-I forms acyl-carnitine, translocase moves it into the matrix, CPT-II regenerates acyl-CoA; CPT-I is the regulated step inhibited by malonyl-CoA
Cycle step 1: acyl-CoA dehydrogenase produces FADH2
Cycle step 2: enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water; step 3: 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase produces NADH
Step 4: thiolase cleaves off acetyl-CoA, leaving acyl-CoA two carbons shorter
Cycle repeats (n/2 - 1 times); acetyl-CoA enters the citric acid cycle or is used for ketone bodies, and FADH2/NADH feed the respiratory chain
questions.explanation: Fatty acids are activated, carried into mitochondria by the carnitine shuttle and then shortened by repeated four-step cycles. Each cycle releases one acetyl-CoA, one FADH2 and one NADH, which supply the citric acid cycle and respiratory chain.

questions.stem: Contrast the location, key enzyme, coenzymes and hormonal regulation of fatty acid synthesis with those of fatty acid oxidation, and explain how the two pathways are prevented from running at the same time. Then describe how ketone bodies are made in the liver of a fasting person.
markingGuide: Synthesis: acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, uses malonyl-CoA and NADPH, activated by insulin and citrate; oxidation: CPT-I regulated, produces FADH2 and NADH, favoured by glucagon and fasting
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I so that newly made fatty acids are not oxidised
Fasting: low insulin and high glucagon release fatty acids; oxaloacetate diverted to gluconeogenesis so acetyl-CoA accumulates

Ketogenesis in liver mitochondria: two acetyl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA (thiolase), then HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase), then acetoacetate (HMG-CoA lyase); beta-hydroxybutyrate via NADH-dependent reduction; acetone by decarboxylation
Ketone bodies are used by muscle, heart and brain; liver lacks thiophorase
questions.explanation: Because synthesis and oxidation occupy different compartments and use different coenzymes, they can be controlled separately, and malonyl-CoA couples them by blocking CPT-I. In fasting the liver turns the excess acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, fuels that other tissues can oxidise.
